description: A synth-pop escape plan from Taylor Swift's Reputation (2017), written with Jack Antonoff. Swift narrates a rebound romance staged like a Bonnie-and-Clyde getaway — thrilling, doomed, and gone before the sirens fade.

pops.text: Track 9 on Reputation (2017) — the album's great escape fantasy, built on pulsing synths and programmed drums.
Swift wrote and produced this one with Jack Antonoff, her go-to collaborator for late-night synth-pop.
That's Swift's own voice treated with distortion and vocoder effects in the opening — a long way from country radio.
The song cruises at about 86 beats per minute in C major, then shifts up to D major shortly after the two-minute mark for the final getaway.
Bonnie and Clyde get name-checked: the narrator slips out of one relationship and straight into a rebound, riding in the getaway car.
It was recorded at Rough Customer Studio in Brooklyn Heights, with Laura Sisk engineering.
A 'making of' clip captured Swift and Antonoff nailing down the bridge in roughly 30 seconds. Some escapes really are that fast.
It became a single only in Australia and New Zealand, released September 7, 2018, to support the Reputation Stadium Tour's Australasian leg — and went multi-platinum in both.
Rolling Stone's Rob Sheffield ranked it No. 13 in his 2019 rundown of Taylor Swift's songs.
No official music video exists — Swift told fans at Paris radio station NRJ in 2019 there wouldn't be one. On the Eras Tour she performed it with Antonoff in East Rutherford in 2023.

title: Getaway Car

description: Greg Humphreys' swooning Smiths homage from Dillon Fence's 1989 debut EP — a Chapel Hill college-rock gem Indy Week dubbed "the crush song" that Hootie & the Blowfish later covered live.

pops.text: Meet Frances. Greg Humphreys wrote her — the swooning centerpiece of Dillon Fence's self-titled debut EP, released in 1989 on NOCAR Records.
It opens with an apology: "Pardon me, Frances, for I have sinned." Confession first, jangle immediately after.
Popdose called it a near-perfect three-and-a-half-minute tribute to the Smiths — the band nails the Marr/Joyce/Rourke sound while Humphreys goes deeper-voiced than Morrissey.
The EP version clocks in at 3:28. Short, lovesick, and built to be replayed — very Chapel Hill, very 1989.
Indy Week gave it the perfect nickname: "the crush song." One listen and the diagnosis is hard to argue with.
Dillon Fence formed in 1986 at UNC-Chapel Hill, originally calling themselves the Magoos before their first gig forced a rename.
The band's name comes from a regionally famous fence built by local artists in Dillon, South Carolina. Yes, an actual fence.
In 1990 the song crossed over to a wider audience as track 3 on FrequeNCy, Mammoth Records' sampler of the rising North Carolina scene.
Famous fans alert: Hootie & the Blowfish have covered "Frances" live. Hootie used to open for Dillon Fence — later, the order flipped.
When the band assembled its 2004 best-of Best +, "Frances" made disc 1 — sourced straight from this 1989 EP recording. Some first takes can't be improved.

title: Frances

description: The funky-jangle opener of Dillon Fence's 1989 self-released EP, re-cut for their Mammoth Records debut Rosemary (1992). A Chapel Hill cult favorite whose falsetto hook fans still sing back at reunion shows.

pops.text: This is the opening track of Dillon Fence's self-titled 1989 EP, released on the band's own NOCAR Records.
The band formed in 1986 at UNC–Chapel Hill — and originally called themselves the Magoos.
Their name came from a landmark outsider-art fence in Dillon, South Carolina, spotted shortly before their first show.
Singer-guitarist Greg Humphreys is the band's principal songwriter — and the voice behind that falsetto intro.
Popdose summed up the EP version as 'funky jangle' — jangly guitars with a little strut underneath.
The EP did its job: the buzz helped Dillon Fence sign with North Carolina's Mammoth Records in 1991.
The song returned on the band's first full album, Rosemary, released February 11, 1992 — the version heard in this video.
On Rosemary, the track leans into '70s disco-rock and funk guitar grooves, per Cryptic Rock's 25th-anniversary revisit of the album.
Rosemary producer Ron Saint Germain arrived with a serious résumé: he had engineered Living Colour's Vivid and produced Sonic Youth's Goo.
At the band's 2000 reunion show at Cat's Cradle in Carrboro, the crowd chimed in on the falsetto intro — Indy Week was there to report it.

title: Something For You

description: The riff-driven rocker from Dillon Fence's 1989 debut EP — spelled "For Awhile" back then — that became the band's go-to live opener and leads off their 2004 best-of, Best +.

pops.text: Spot the typo that stuck: on the band's 1989 debut EP this was spelled "For Awhile" — one word. It sits at track 4, running 3:49.
Popdose singled it out as one of the EP's rockers — while its neighbors jangled, "For Awhile" leaned into a tougher rock frame of mind.
The writing team behind the jangle: singer-guitarist Greg Humphreys and bassist Chris Goode had been playing together since high school.
Dillon Fence formed at UNC-Chapel Hill in 1986 — Humphreys, Goode, guitarist Kent Alphin and drummer Brooke Pitts, first calling themselves the Magoos.
Fifteen years later, the spelling got fixed: as "For A While" it opens Best +, the band's 2004 double-disc best-of. Track 1, disc 1 — statement made.
Best + arrived September 7, 2004: 18 remastered favorites plus brand-new songs, with the original lineup back together to record them.
Why lead with a 1989 EP cut? Greg Humphreys told Goldmine in 2024 that the band has used this song as its live opener, off and on, for years.
December 22, 2000, Cat's Cradle reunion show: Indy Week reported the crowd "went berserk" the moment this song's riff kicked in.
The opener tradition held: "For A While" also kicks off In Flagrante Delicto, the reunited band's 2024 live album, stretching to 4:25 on stage.
From EP track 4 in 1989 to first song on the best-of and the live album — not bad for a song that started life with a spelling mistake.

title: For A While

description: The lead single from David Bowie's Tonight (1984): a lean, Eddie Cochran-inspired rocker that hit the Top 10 on both sides of the Atlantic. Its 21-minute film Jazzin' for Blue Jean won Bowie a Grammy.

pops.text: The lead single from Tonight (1984), Bowie's 16th studio album — cut down to a lean 3 minutes and 8 seconds.
It's one of only two songs on Tonight written entirely by Bowie. The other is 'Loving the Alien.'
Recorded in May 1984 at Le Studio in Morin-Heights, Quebec, and co-produced by Bowie, Derek Bramble and Hugh Padgham.
Bowie loosely modeled the song on Eddie Cochran — straight-ahead rock and roll, no concept album attached.
Chart report: No. 6 in the UK and No. 8 in the US — Bowie's fifth, and last, American Top 10 solo hit.
The song launched with a 21-minute short film, Jazzin' for Blue Jean, directed by Julien Temple.
Bowie plays both leads in the film: Vic, an ordinary guy trying to impress a date, and preening rock star Screamin' Lord Byron.
Jazzin' for Blue Jean won the 1985 Grammy Award for Best Video, Short Form.
It was the only competitive Grammy Bowie won during his lifetime — his next ones came posthumously, for Blackstar.
Three versions of the video exist — the full short film, a three-minute performance edit and an alternate MTV cut — all gathered on the Best of Bowie DVD.

title: Blue Jean

description: Bowie teamed with Chic's Nile Rodgers for a sleek dance-rock smash that topped charts on both sides of the Atlantic. Its Australia-shot video turned a pop hit into a statement on race and consumerism.

pops.text: Fresh start, clear brief: this was Bowie's first album for EMI after years on RCA, and he reportedly told producer Nile Rodgers of Chic, 'I really want you to make hits.'
It was recorded at the Power Station in New York, co-produced by Bowie and Rodgers. Chic's sleek funk, rebuilt for rock radio, is the engine under the whole track.
That huge opening guitar sound was an accident. Engineer Bob Clearmountain set a tape delay too loud, jumped to fix it — and Bowie and Rodgers shouted that it was exactly right.
Bowie had been blown away by a young Texas blues guitarist at the 1982 Montreux Jazz Festival. His name? Stevie Ray Vaughan — and Bowie brought him to New York to play.
Vaughan plays the closing solo, largely unknown at the time. Later in 1983 his own debut album, Texas Flood, made him a star in his own right.
Vaughan was set to join Bowie's Serious Moonlight tour — named for a lyric in this song — but quit just days before the first date over pay and musical fit.

Director David Mallet shot the video in Australia, in a pub in Carinda, New South Wales, and in Warrumbungle National Park. Its stars were Terry Roberts and Joelene King, students from Sydney's Aboriginal Islander Dance Theatre.
Bowie called the video a direct statement against racism and oppression. The magical red shoes nod to Hans Christian Andersen's tale — and, Bowie said, symbolised striving within capitalist society.
In the UK it entered the chart at No. 5 and climbed to No. 1, staying there for three weeks. It finished 1983 as one of Britain's biggest-selling singles of the year.

On 21 May 1983 it hit No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, knocking Michael Jackson's 'Beat It' off the top — Bowie's first single to top both the US and UK charts, and the best-selling single of his career.

title: Let's Dance

description: Bowie's tale of doomed astronaut Major Tom, rush-released days before Apollo 11, became his first hit. Its title plays on Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey, and Major Tom haunted his work for decades.

pops.text: The title is a pun on Stanley Kubrick's 1968 film 2001: A Space Odyssey, which Bowie saw and drew on for this tale of an astronaut drifting beyond help.
Producer Tony Visconti refused to make it, calling it a cheap shot cashing in on the Moon shot. So engineer Gus Dudgeon stepped up and produced Bowie's breakthrough instead.
Recorded on 20 June 1969 at Trident Studios in London, with Paul Buckmaster arranging the orchestra. Future Yes star Rick Wakeman plays the Mellotron.

Listen for the beeping, floating sounds near the end: that's Bowie himself on a Stylophone, a tiny toy synth played with a pen. Bassist Herbie Flowers and Pentangle drummer Terry Cox anchor the launch.
It was rush-released on 11 July 1969 — five days before Apollo 11 launched. The BBC then used it as background music during its television coverage of the Moon landing.
America caught up later: a 1973 reissue reached No. 15 on the Billboard Hot 100, giving Bowie his first US hit single, three years after the song was new.
Second time was the charm at home, too: a 1975 UK reissue finally took 'Space Oddity' to No. 1 — the first UK chart-topper of Bowie's career.
This video came later: photographer Mick Rock filmed Bowie miming to the 1969 recording in New York in December 1972, during the Aladdin Sane sessions, to promote that US reissue.
Major Tom never really left. Bowie brought him back in 'Ashes to Ashes' in 1980, again in 'Hallo Spaceboy,' and an astronaut's skeleton appears in the 'Blackstar' video near the end of Bowie's life.
In 2013 astronaut Chris Hadfield performed it aboard the International Space Station — the first music video recorded in space. Bowie called it possibly the most poignant version ever created.

title: Space Oddity

description: A swaggering Page-Plant rocker begun in a Welsh cottage in 1970, recorded for Houses of the Holy, then shelved until Jimmy Page added overdubs and rescued it for the double album Physical Graffiti.

pops.text: It started quietly: Page and Plant began writing this song in 1970 at Bron-Yr-Aur, the remote Welsh cottage where they retreated to write. At first, it was an acoustic piece.
The band cut the electric version in May 1972 at Stargroves, using the Rolling Stones' mobile studio, during sessions for Houses of the Holy. Then they left it off that album.
Page revived the tape in 1974, adding several guitar overdubs at Olympic Studios. That rescue job earned it a place on Physical Graffiti in 1975.

The album's liner notes joke about this track: 'Guitar lost courtesy of Ron Nevison, salvaged by the grace of Keith Harwood.' Page later said an engineer had erased one of its guitar tracks during overdubbing.
Page pointed to this song as the purest example of the band's swagger, name-checking rockabilly pioneer Link Wray as the attitude he wanted the guitar to carry.
On Physical Graffiti it sits second, right after 'Custard Pie' — a one-two opening punch for Led Zeppelin's sprawling 15-track double album.
Physical Graffiti, released 24 February 1975, was the band's first album on their own Swan Song Records label, after their Atlantic deal ended.
That famous cover is a New York tenement at 96 and 98 St. Mark's Place, its windows die-cut so the inner sleeves show through. One floor was removed from the photo to fit the square sleeve.
Here's the oddity: Led Zeppelin never performed 'The Rover' in full in concert. On the 1977 tour, audiences only got its opening riff, used as an intro into 'Sick Again.'
Shelved for one album, nearly damaged in another session, never fully played live — and still a fan favourite. Some songs really do earn the name 'Rover' by surviving the journey.

title: The Rover

description: The explosive opener to Houses of the Holy began life as an instrumental overture meant to flow into 'The Rain Song.' Plant added lyrics about life on tour, and the title later named Zeppelin's concert film.

pops.text: This opens Houses of the Holy, released 28 March 1973 — the first Led Zeppelin album with a title that wasn't simply the band's name.
It wasn't meant to have words at all. Page built it as an instrumental called 'The Overture,' designed to segue straight into 'The Rain Song.'
Plant heard it and insisted it was too good to be just a doorway: better get some lyrics — quick. For a while, with words about touring, it was titled 'The Campaign.'
Page said that once Plant suggested dropping into half-time in the middle, the whole song came together in a day, assembled from bits of ideas on his ever-present cassette recorder.
It was recorded on 18 May 1972 at Stargroves with the Rolling Stones' mobile truck. Page played the backing track on a Fender electric 12-string, with Les Paul overdubs on top.
Hear how urgent Plant sounds? His vocal track was slightly sped up for the album, pushing it a touch higher than he actually sang it in the studio.
The band first played it live on their 1972 Japanese tour — before Houses of the Holy was even out, and before the song had settled on its final title.
On stage, this became a showcase for Page's Gibson double-neck guitar, letting him handle the 12-string parts and 6-string parts in one song without swapping instruments.
The title outgrew the track: The Song Remains the Same became the name of the band's 1976 concert film and its soundtrack album, filmed at Madison Square Garden in July 1973.
Want to hear Page's original plan? The deluxe reissue of Houses of the Holy includes an instrumental reference mix, showing the overture as it existed before Plant sang a word.

title: The Song Remains the Same

description: Jimmy Page's gentle solo acoustic instrumental, named for the Welsh cottage where Led Zeppelin III was born. Recorded in 1970 and held for five years, it is the shortest studio recording the band ever released.

pops.text: No singer, no band — just Jimmy Page and an acoustic guitar. Plant once introduced it by explaining that Bron-Yr-Aur is the little cottage in the mountains of Snowdonia, and the Welsh for 'Golden Breast.'

That cottage, on the outskirts of Machynlleth, was a Plant family holiday spot from his childhood. In spring 1970, after a gruelling American tour, Page and Plant retreated there — to a cottage with no running water and no electricity — to write.
Page recorded this piece in July 1970 at Island Studios in London, during the sessions for Led Zeppelin III. Beautiful as it is, it didn't make that album.
So it waited. When Physical Graffiti needed older material to fill a double album, this was the oldest recording chosen — finally released on 24 February 1975, nearly five years after it was cut.
It is the only track on Physical Graffiti credited to Page alone. Fifteen songs, four band members — and this quiet moment belongs to one man and six strings.
At about two minutes, it is Led Zeppelin's shortest studio recording. The same album also holds their longest, 'In My Time of Dying,' at over eleven minutes — extremes, side by side.
Mind the spelling: this is 'Bron-Yr-Aur,' with a Y. Led Zeppelin III has a different, rowdier song called 'Bron-Y-Aur Stomp' — same cottage, very different energy.
Part of its glow is the tuning: Page plays in an open C6 tuning (C-A-C-G-C-E), which lets the notes ring into each other like light through cottage windows.

It surfaced live only occasionally, in the band's acoustic sets on their summer 1970 tour. Its afterlife has been quieter and longer: decades later it was included in Cameron Crowe's Almost Famous soundtrack collection.
Two minutes, recorded in a hurry of inspiration in 1970, kept in a drawer for five years. Some pieces don't need words, a chorus, or length — just a place worth remembering.

title: Bron-Yr-Aur

description: A late-night drum-machine groove from the Private Eyes album that became Hall & Oates' fourth No. 1 — and one of the most borrowed basslines in pop, R&B and hip-hop.

pops.text: This one started after hours! Once the Private Eyes sessions cleared out of New York's Electric Lady Studios, Hall, Oates and engineer Neil Kernon stayed behind with the gear still on.
That beat is a preset, not a drummer. Hall hit 'Rock and Roll 1' on an old Roland CompuRhythm drum machine and started playing along.
The famous bassline came to Hall on a Korg organ sitting nearby. He said the chords came together in about 10 minutes.
Plot twist: it is not really a lover Hall is refusing. He has said the song is about being manipulated by management and the music business.
Listen for Charles DeChant's saxophone solo cutting through the synths. His playing is the track's slinky, soulful counterweight.
Chart climb: released as the second single from Private Eyes, it reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 on January 30, 1982 — the duo's fourth No. 1.
It also topped Billboard's R&B and dance charts, a rare crossover feat for a white act at the time. One groove, three different No. 1s.
At the 'We Are the World' session in 1985, Michael Jackson told Hall he had borrowed this groove for 'Billie Jean.' Hall shrugged: it's something we all do.
Hip-hop heard it too. De La Soul built their 1989 anti-drug track 'Say No Go' around a sample of this song's hook.
Simply Red went further in 2003: their UK No. 7 hit 'Sunrise' was built heavily on this track's instrumentation, with Hall & Oates credited as songwriters.

title: I Can't Go for That (No Can Do)

description: The title track of Hall & Oates' tenth album, built on a handclap hook and a detective joke. It spent two weeks at No. 1 in November 1981 and became an early MTV staple.

pops.text: The title came from a roadside billboard. Songwriter Warren Pash saw an ad for The Private Eyes, a 1980 Tim Conway and Don Knotts detective comedy, while driving in Los Angeles.
Pash and Janna Allen wrote most of the song — and it was first meant for Janna, who hoped to launch a singing career of her own.
Change of plans: about a month later, Janna decided the song was not for her, but was perfect for Daryl and John — so she gave them the cassette.
Hall then changed the chords and rearranged it, and he and Sara Allen wrote the lyrics. All four — Pash, Hall and both Allen sisters — share the credit; Oates has none on this one.
It is the title track and lead single from the duo's tenth studio album, Private Eyes, recorded at Electric Lady Studios in New York.
That chorus hook is pure handclaps — clap-clap. Simple, punchy, and impossible to hear just once.
It hit No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 on November 7, 1981, and stayed for two weeks — the duo's third of six career No. 1 singles.
Olivia Newton-John's 'Physical' succeeded it at No. 1. A few months later Hall & Oates took the top spot back when 'I Can't Go for That' knocked 'Physical' out.
Video time: director Jay Dubin shot the clip on the spur of the moment at Electric Lady, on a small budget in a few hours — the band simply dressed as old-time gumshoes.
Hall & Oates earned their first Grammy nomination, for Best Pop Vocal Performance by a Duo or Group, for 'Private Eyes.'

title: Private Eyes

description: A breezy Voices single that was never meant for Hall & Oates at all. Written for someone else as a quick demo, it became their second No. 1 and spent three weeks on top.

pops.text: Co-writer Janna Allen was the younger sister of Sara Allen, Hall's longtime girlfriend. Hall has said Janna wrote most of this song.
It was one of the first songs Janna had ever written — and she wrote it for herself, hoping to start a singing career.
As a favour, Hall cut a quick demo with just drum machine and piano, so Janna would have a guide version to sing from.
That demo almost never made the album. Once their manager and others heard it, everyone insisted it belonged on Voices — so the demo became the basis of the finished track.
The band fleshed the demo out with guitar and vocals rather than re-recording it from scratch. The simple guide take is still at the song's core.
It was the third single from their ninth album, Voices (1980) — the album where Hall & Oates took control and produced themselves.
Hall calls it an anti-love song. The kiss is not the whole world — it is just one item, tongue-in-cheek, on a list of other things he likes.
Misheard for decades: many listeners swear he sings 'your kiss is on my lips.' The word is 'list' — which is exactly the joke.
It topped the Billboard Hot 100 on April 11, 1981, and spent three weeks at No. 1 — their second No. 1, after 'Rich Girl' in 1977.
Its video was among those aired on MTV's very first day of broadcast, August 1, 1981 — helping a demo that almost stayed in a drawer become inescapable.

title: Kiss on My List

description: Rumours' patchwork anthem, stitched from rejected pieces by all five band members. Never a single, it became their signature opener, a Formula 1 theme and a movie anthem.

pops.text: Group project, literally: 'The Chain' is the only song on Rumours credited to all five members of the band's classic line-up.
It began as a Christine McVie song called 'Butter Cookie (Keep Me There).' The start was not working, but the band loved its ending.
Nothing went to waste. Buckingham recycled the intro from 'Lola (My Love),' a song from the 1973 Buckingham Nicks album.
Engineers Ken Caillat and Richard Dashut assembled the track at the Record Plant in Sausalito — at times manually splicing tape with a razor blade.
Because it was spliced together, drums and guitar were reportedly the only instruments on Rumours recorded in each other's company on this track.
Stevie Nicks supplied the verse lyrics, written about her crumbling relationship with Lindsey Buckingham — hence 'never break the chain.'
Wait for the shift around three minutes in: John McVie's thundering bass line, built with Mick Fleetwood, was originally meant for a different song.
Surprise: for all its fame, 'The Chain' was never released as a single from Rumours. Radio, concerts and TV made it a hit anyway.
In Britain that bass outro became the sound of speed — the BBC used it as its Formula 1 theme from 1978 to 1996, then again from 2009 to 2015.
New century, new audience: the song powers key moments in Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 (2017), and a live version from The Dance had already charted in 1997.

title: The Chain

description: Stevie Nicks' gentle answer to a breakup, written in about 10 minutes on Rumours. It is Fleetwood Mac's only US No. 1 — and, decades later, a viral hit all over again.

pops.text: Solo credit: Stevie Nicks wrote 'Dreams' entirely by herself, and she sings lead on it too.
She wrote it in about 10 minutes, sitting on a big black-velvet bed in a spare Record Plant room in Sausalito said to have been built for Sly Stone.
Her tools were minimal: a keyboard, a drum pattern she found, and a little cassette recorder switched on to catch the idea.
The lyric is her side of her split with Lindsey Buckingham. Where his 'Go Your Own Way' slams the door, Nicks has said her heart in 'Dreams' stayed open and hopeful.
Christine McVie was not sold at first, calling the piano demo boring — just a few chords and one note in the left hand.
Buckingham proved her wrong by fashioning three distinct sections out of the same chords, so each part of the song feels completely different.
Released as Rumours' second single in March 1977, it reached No. 1 on June 18 — for one week, and it remains Fleetwood Mac's only US No. 1 single.
No big production for the promo: a stage performance of 'Dreams' was used as its promotional music video.
Rolling Stone ranked it No. 9 on its 2021 list of the 500 Greatest Songs of All Time — the highest debut for a song absent from the original list.
Then came TikTok: in 2020 Nathan Apodaca longboarded, sipped Ocean Spray Cran-Raspberry and lip-synced to 'Dreams.' It re-entered the Hot 100 and climbed to No. 12, 43 years after No. 1.

title: Dreams
